(Folio 1a) (Line 1) The nature of mantras is the noose of passion (*rāgapāśa*)... [or] the noose of attachment (*saṅgapāśa*)... (Line 2) It would be the noose of passion (*rāgapāśa*) and the noose of attachment (*saṅgapāśa*)... [and] the noose of ignorance (*avidyāpāśa*)... [of] the great heart... (Line 3)
The flow of the essences (*sara*) is the flow of the *piṇḍas*. The channel (*nāḍī*) is among the channels; and that which is called power (*śakti*) is the bond (*pāśa*).
And may there be auspiciousness for me. Among all things, the bond of Śiva (*śivapāśa*) is proclaimed as being in the midst of all.
I salute the feet of the venerable Guru, [the leader of the Gaṇas] (*...*) Gaṇanāyaka. (5th line) For the sake of accomplishing the meaning of the Śiva Āgamas, I salute Skandaguru (*...*).
Even though all actions are eternal (*nitya-sarva-karmāṇi*), there is no worship [without him] (*...*) (*...*)ṇa. (6th line)
And specifically for the consecration of temples, sacrificial altars, liṅgas, images, and so forth;
thereafter [the purification of] the site, the construction, and following that, the worship of the door.
The seat for the image and the image itself, as well as the *liṅga*,
should first be placed upon the bathing altar for the purpose of bathing.
[The performance of] the nyāsa upon him and his dismissal;
then, for the sake of Caṇḍeśa, one should specially provide the oil massage and other services.

The purification of the *liṅga* and the pedestal (*pīṭha*), as well as the seat (*āsana*) itself; having then conceived the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*), one follows the sequence beginning with the bath and the womb (*garbha*).
Subsequently, [one should contemplate] the very place situated upon the lotus throne;
then follows the sequence of the five seats.
The invocation and so forth...
and the bali offering as well.
Daily [worship]... and worship on the following day as well; thereafter, incense and lamps, and then likewise the bali offering.
Daily [worship]... in this manner, or even for five nights.
Until nightfall, one should likewise [apply] the ash and the triple [mark].
The parasols, yak-tail whisks, and clusters of lotuses;
likewise, the Vedas, the Purāṇas, and the Itihāsas.
[The offering] consisting of hearing, dance, song, and instrumental music combined;
and likewise, the recitation of that [mantra] and its dedication.
Furthermore, the limb of *laya* (rhythm), and again the [recitation of the] *puṣpagaṇa* (flower-cluster) [mantra], which is the essence of the *śikhā*.
[The measurement] is one *kārdaka* [in length].
(Second line: Afterwards, [one should perform] worship especially within the supreme, subtle reality (*tattva*) of Śiva.
[Obeisance] to you there, [the most excellent] darkness... (3rd line) ...and likewise Caṇḍa... behind.
She is a vessel for circumambulation and salutation;
therefore, one should not cause oneself to be like a bitter gourd.
Afterwards, the proclamation of the Dharma (*dharmasaṃkīrtana*) [should be performed], filling [the space]... Thus, according to the path taught in the scriptures, [one should act].
O worshipper, one should perform everything in this manner.
(........... it is declared that one should practice this until the end of life. [Thus, in the *Candratājñāna*.]
[Daily Worship]
[Now I shall describe the daily worship (*nityārcana*), which bestows all accomplishments... (7th line) [... it is established in every *liṅga*.

Therefore, one should worship [the deity] in the *liṅga*. The God himself is directly present there; he who is established in grace should be worshipped in the *liṅga*. That man who does not worship him—the Lord of the Three Worlds—does not obtain great fortune, nor heaven, nor liberation, nor sovereignty.
A person with a family should always worship the Liṅga, which accomplishes all goals.

(4th line) Therefore, becoming single-minded, for as long as one lives, having shown compassion toward the Great One... even though we are [sinful], the wise man should always [worship]. (5th line) It is better to give up one’s life than to ever fail to worship the supreme God once; having worshipped Him, one should not fear Lord Śiva, the husband of Umā. (6th line)

Having killed [a human] with human skin while performing recitation (*japa*) and the worship of Śiva, he—having cast aside doubt—[eats] the *liṅga*...; that man who [acts] like a crow at the time of death goes to hell, his hair [standing on end], excluded from devotion (*bhakti*). Day after day, [he eats] the impurity... and so forth. Without having worshipped [it], there is no atonement for that sin.
Those who worship with great effort...
(3rd line) ...twenty [merits] emerge from the worship of the *liṅga*... (4th line)

There is no doubt regarding the attainment of the fruit. By reciting [the name] out of praise, curiosity, [ignorance], or [whatever else], a mortal is liberated from all sins. [Whatever other... merit there may be elsewhere than the worship of the Liṅga—having understood this, [this is] the new [practice]... (... by deluding all the gods (... a man would go to hell; for him, [the protection] of Maheśvara (... (2nd line) (...
the entire three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving, [are protected]. O Destroyer of Forms, because of fear of the Creator Maheśvara, among all beings (3rd line) [...]

In all states of existence, one should with every effort bring about only auspiciousness for those who have taken refuge in Śiva. Even if there were oceans [of sins], there is indeed nothing that cannot be overcome; for even for a moment in the world of Rudra, when one has gone for refuge to Śaṅkara, the serpent-like coils of the heart are released through the recollection of his son, and by his grace, the rope of the body is purified by his power.

The merit of all supreme and most excellent knowledge regarding every sin, the fruit of all meritorious gifts given on every lunar day (*tithi*), whatever merit [is gained from] all [other acts], and the fruit of all [these combined]— that fruit is obtained by worshipping Śiva ten million times. Whatever merit is gained from the *Cāndrāyaṇa* [vow], and the merit of hundreds of heated iron spikes [endured], all those merits are attained through the worship of the Liṅga.
or having worshipped [it] even once, human beings attain perfection; the perfected ones go to the city of Śiva and sport for an eon (3rd line).

[This is] the earth-world (bhūloka... [and] the seven worlds: the atmospheric world (bhuvarloka), the heavenly world (svarloka), the world of desire (kāmaloka), the world of humans (janaloka), the world of austerity (tapas), and the world of truth (satya). (4th line)

Which [deities] are proclaimed? He who worships them in the *liṅga*—residence in those [worlds] is ordained for him. Even for thousands of millions of births, [he is not born] in the five wombs. When the *liṅga* has been worshipped even once, one is liberated from the cycle of destruction through sacrifice; he who worships it even once...
For three hundred million years on the delightful peak of Kailāsa, [he remained] amidst the mothers and fathers... through the longing for play...
(7th line) whether out of delusion, ostentation, or deceit—in whatever manner he was joined with another, by him [was] Śiva [worshipped]; [thus] was sin committed.

But those among men whose souls are devoted to the worship of the *liṅga*, resembling pure crystal, go to the world [of Śiva]. (... One should remember the sequence [of mantras], being intent on the propitiation of the *liṅga*. Therefore, even a human being attains all [goals] through desire, O Goddess. In this Kali age, you are Kapālī; you are the seer (*ṛṣi*); you are the god; you are the source of bliss for the gods. (... may there be [success] for you.

By worshipping the *liṅga*... O Goddess, when it is worshipped, [the fruit] is obtained; there is no doubt in this matter. One should worship the *liṅga* with *darbha* grass... on that day, O Sovereign Lady (*Īśvarī*). With hundreds of millions of celestial chariots (*vimāna*), mounted upon the bull (*vṛṣa*), [one attains] the destruction of sins... for the sake of [attaining] the state of the gods.
We pray for the removal of various [obstacles]... in the state of existence (*kṣatratva*).

not by (..... having attained the state of peace (.. for the sake of meditation (.......... the supreme state (....... the goal (................. through wisdom (pala... ga (3rd line) worship and delight (-)

Having risen at dawn, [one who] worships the Liṅga once with devotion... attains [the fruit]. ... having given [a gift], one would obtain that merit which is acquired when the midday sun has arrived and [one] worships... Having fully worshipped and given the earth... one would attain that [merit]. When the sun has reached the western quarter, one should worship Śiva... [attains]... (6th line).
Whatever fruit there is from not giving away ten million cows, [that fruit is obtained] by [worshipping] the Liṅga, O friend—
[this is the worship at the three times].
Having become pure, one should worship; one obtains the fruit equal to a thousand *agniṣṭoma* sacrifices. Thus, at all times, if a person worships with devotion, he shall attain all desires.
In the morning time... [known by the twice-born...]

The *brahmapraya* is nourishing (*pauṣṭika*). At midday... it has equal fruit... [it] destroys sins... beneficial for Vaiśyas... its entirety... [it is] the end... Rudra’s... [it is] considered... primarily Gaurī’s... the worship of the three sections (*trikhaṇḍa*) is both supreme and middling. The supreme is pure...
For the sake of the goal, the highest [form] is said to be through mantras; the middling is that which is declared in the Śaiva Veda...
my... (F6a, 1st line)... the self and the impurity... worship is said to be twofold. And the vision of Rudra... (2nd line)... the world... mā...

It is stretched out on a permanent altar, or specifically on a temporary maṇḍala, or on a portable image, or particularly on a temporary one; this is known as the worship for a specific purpose (*atārthayajana*). The *liṅga* is of six kinds: made of stone, made of jewels, made of bell-metal, made of metal, made of wood, and likewise made of clay or temporary.

[He] is liberated. Having fashioned a gem of nine kinds and a stone of eight [kinds], [the installation is] fivefold. For a treasure-chest, that which is made of wood is of nine kinds; likewise, the *liṅga* and its image are of two types for the purpose of installation (*pratiṣṭhā*). [The gems are]: ruby, pearl, diamond, sapphire, lapis lazuli, emerald, topaz, and crystal.
These are indeed not corals, nor are they gems. On the stone slab...

[they appear] red-hued, yellow, and black; these should be applied to the Brahmins and the other castes respectively. Among those who follow the favorable [signs], the black one should be accepted for all castes and fashioned as auspicious silver; that copper-colored one is a slayer.
For the sake of the apūraka-heap, [the materials] including the moonstone and the elements for the linga are said by the Sage to be eightfold and pure:

*viṣṇu*, *bilva*, *aśmanti* (*aśmantaka*), *candana*, and *devadāru*; for the purpose of the linga, the trees *aśvattha* and *karañja* are used, as well as *plakṣa* and *khadira* among the trees suitable for making it.
The nine mango trees are said to be with sap; one should release various types of clay for the sake of stability. This is the undifferentiated linga.
I shall now describe its consecration and its forms; listen to that which must be done by the artisan here.

And for the sake of the establishment of the Pāṭaliṅga [temple], once that [foundation] has been accomplished, having purified that [land] in the Brahmadeśa region... (7th line)... in the three-footed [space]... by whom was it sprinkled? A ritual image of Viṣṇu is to be made; you shall become the milk-ocean for both [the worlds]. [The offering consists of] wheat, black gram, and other grains mixed with... oil... (7a, 1st line).

Having cast [the ingredients] into the crucible and added the essence, one should churn it with a ladle and fashion the linga according to the prescribed characteristics. Having prepared [the mixture] in the month of Āśvina, one should fashion the linga from these five substances using the *iṣa* [ladle]. It is both mobile and known as immobile; the mobile [linga]...
And likewise the Śaiva portion: from one *tāla* down to one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*), the food-liṅga (*annaliṅga*) is mobile and excellent;

that which is immobile is a liṅga suitable for a temple or a marketplace. The excellent [liṅga] should be of its own [appropriate] material, the middling one of gold, and the inferior one should have a silver pedestal; in the absence of that, however—

[It should be] made of copper. In its absence, there may be a stone [liṅga]; for a jewel-liṅga, there should be a pedestal (*pīṭhikā*). The channel (*nāḍī*) should be equal to the length, and the pedestal (*pīṭha*) should be equal to that. One should specifically make the height of the pedestal equal to the width of the head; it should be fashioned according to one's own heart’s desire. When the liṅga is divided into four parts, three parts are said to be visible. The pedestal should be fixed and immovable.

And one should have that made: cow-dung (*gomaya*), a ball of cow-muck (*gosakṛt-piṇḍa*), ash, and the fibers of *unnābha* grass; ground *panita*, a brush of sandalwood (*candana-kūrcaka*), flowers, sand (*sikatā*), and sprouts (*pallava*). However, for those lingas that are intended to be momentary (*kṣaṇika*), there is no fixed rule (*lakṣaṇa*) at all. At the conclusion of the worship, their removal (*uddhāra*) is prescribed. [Various... (5th line)

[The temple] is joined with [parts] that are broken, endowed with various obstructions, and [filled] with gravel and so forth; [it is] not [proper]. (6th line) ... even all of that is proclaimed as such. For the anointing of the head... in the middle of that, there is no measurement (*māna*) whatsoever that is seen; rather, the measurement is prescribed according to the proportions of the palace. (F8a, 1st line)

One should worship with devotion a Liṅga made of jewels, O Lakṣmī... [he] would worship... (2nd line) ...a Liṅga made of gold... [he] would give. By that, Soma also, having attained the state of Soma, [bestows] water constantly. A Liṅga made of diamond... always... (3rd line) ...those Mothers likewise. Their motherhood is established; they all go to the supreme station. A Liṅga made of... one should worship according to the rule... (4th line) ...he would give.
You are Viṣṇu, the one whose speech is bestowed; he is that eternal thread (*sanātana*). Bṛhaspati...

[the] *liṅga* produced from lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*)... should be worshipped as having attained equality with [him]. He is the destroyer of [sins]... Agastya... even the Great-Souled One (*mahātmā*)...

One should worship with devotion the auspicious linga made of emerald (*haritāśman*), which encompasses all classes; [by doing so] Agastya... [one attains... One should worship with a mind full of devotion that linga made of topaz (*puṣyarāga*), which is enchanting to the sages (*muni*); by that, one shall attain the state of a sage. [One should worship] the stainless crystal (*sphaṭika*)... [line 1].

The *liṅga* is always said to belong to Varuṇa; by that [act], he indeed attained the state of being the one who chooses (*varaṇatva*), endowed with [all] desires. The *liṅga* made of coral, which grants victory and is adorned by the best of serpents—by that [worship], the Nāgas, rich in great enjoyments, attained the supreme station. Brahmā always worshipped the white stone *liṅga* with devotion; through that very worship, he attained the highest state of Brahmahood.
Even the high-souled Daśagrīva, having likewise worshipped a linga made of stone, attained the state of Daśagrīva.

Kumbhakarṇa always worshipped that linga made of stone; by that [act], he attained the state of Kumbhakarṇa. Even though he was cursed by the gods, Gajendra constantly worshipped a linga made of black stone there, and thereby attained the state of Śakra.
Because his *liṅga* is never worshipped, he shall not attain the state of *nāda*, nor indeed the *tattva*.

The high-souled Viśvedeva, having offered sacrifice to Hara... shall not attain [his goal]. Those who worship the syllable *Va* together with the *liṅga* according to the prescribed rule—by that means those high-souled ones have attained excellent... (sumanasaḥ).
[He] always [worshipped] the copper *liṅga* with devotion... [and] the Sun-god.
Three times a day... by him... this supreme [state] was attained.
Vāyu constantly worshipped a *liṅga* made of bell-metal; having attained the state of the anus through those [deeds],...
[He] worships the Liṅga consisting of the essence of the Kūṭa-mantra; by that, the best of Asuras, possessed of immeasurable prowess, [attains his goal]. And the high-souled Rākṣasas [worship it].
With iron, Maya always worships the Liṅga with the Śakti-mantra; endowed with a great bed, he shall attain the state of a sage and enjoyments. [He worships] the Liṅga consisting of tin...
The Piśācas worship it; therefore, endowed with growth and prosperity, they attain the supreme state. Rāhu always worships the Liṅga consisting of the sound of the Bilva tree;
by that, Rāhu attains [great power] accompanied by great strength. Ketu constantly worships the Liṅga... [the source of] light, which is Bhava.

Endowed with great heroism, by that one shall attain [the goal]. The *liṅga* made of *malayaja* [sandalwood] is always worshipped; by that, O Nandin, one attains joy and reaches the state of union (*sāyujya*).
[Made of wood]

One should worship with reverence a liṅga made of *devadāru* wood; by that, one shall attain the status of a leader of the Gaṇas, a station beyond the reach of the [other] Gaṇas. The two high-souled ones [Narada and Parvata] worshipped the liṅga of Vasiṣṭha, born from the *aśvattha* tree; by always [worshipping it], one shall attain the state of Vasiṣṭha. The great sage Viśvāmitra [worshipped] the liṅga born from the *karañja* tree.

One should worship constantly; by that, O hero, one shall attain [the state of] Vīra... [one shall obtain] the fruit arising from [the merit of] hundreds... one should worship the Liṅga with devotion and... according to the prescribed rite, daily... [he spoke of] the boundless... Māṇḍavya, the great sage, spoke of the Liṅga... those who [worship] for the sake of the two-fold purpose, by that... he spoke of peace... having worshipped the Pārtha-liṅga in the [month of] Aśvina... [one attains]... (The text provided is fragmentary; this translation reflects the available portions.)

Renouncing the body after touching the deity... [the heart] through effort... they go... (2nd line) ...accordingly. There, those who worship... [they]... even once... for them, the state of a *piśāca*... (3rd line)

To whomsoever he grants enjoyments, and to those who worship Rudra with eyes [like his], Śiva bestows great enjoyments upon them in this world. To those devoted to their duties for three fortnights... [he grants]... enjoyments.

In the world of Śiva, Śiva bestows upon him [his] desires... even though he is attached to enjoyments... for the sake of progeny, Śiva bestows enjoyments upon him in that world. Those devoted to the eight-fold worship with the *tri-gāyatrī*... through that state of being...

Śiva bestows the world of Brahmā upon them. Those who do not worship Rudra three times [daily], being intent on [worldly] pleasures, go to [the realm of] Bhava; they enjoy divine delights in the celestial abodes, yet they are devoid of devotion to Śiva. They obtain great enjoyment for nine [lifetimes].

In Śivapura, [an image made of] *tulā* (mercury) [bestows] cow-dung [as a fruit]; for the Lord of the Mountain (*Īśāna*), [an image of] cow-horn yields the fruit of cattle. Ashes remove [all] afflictions and likewise grant long life; an image of grain (*annaliṅga*) [bestows] strength and the fulfillment of one's desires. An image of clay (*gaula*) bestows cooked food; copper destroys enmity, and bell-metal (*venika*) bestows happiness.
One should know that ground [sandalwood] bestows nourishment, while sandalwood [in its natural state] bestows progeny.
A brush (kūrca) is said to grant health, and a flower shall bestow fame.
A garland bestows all desires, and it shall bestow strength.
Sand [is auspicious] when it is free from [impurities], and a sprout bestows the six virtues.
(6th line) A consecrated, momentary *liṅga* is said to be "self-arisen" (*svayamudbhūta*). That which has the shape of an umbrella belongs to Indra; that of Agni is uneven at its summit. (7th line)
The tip of the trident is declared to belong to Yama;

that which has the form of a jar is for the Nairṛtas; and that which has the form of a banner is for Varuṇa. The head of the one shaped like a mace should be in the form of a trident, belonging to Soma.
The linga of Īśāna is at the head of the Brāhmaṇa-pada.
These are the characteristics of the disciple of the Vaiṣṇava [lineage] (*),
as well as by others— gods, Daityas, Dānavas, Indras, and Niśācaras.
And by the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and others, as well as by other lords of the Gaṇas—
[having] established or having caused [it] to be established— the Liṅga was worshipped.
[The Characteristics of the Pīṭha]
Now, the self-arisen division of the seats (pīṭha) is indicated among the heads:
the first shall be the Padmapīṭha, and the second the Bhadrapīṭha.
The third is named Śrīkara, and the fourth is Niśvāsa;
one should know the fifth as Vijaya, and the sixth is remembered as Svāyaṃbhuva. One should know the seventh as Saṃpad, and the eighth is Svastika.
The ninth should be the full moon, and the tenth would be the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila).
The twelfth is called Vajra, named after Rudra;
the thirteenth is Vimalatā, and these are the thirteen seats.
A triangular [stone] is to be known as a bestower of boons; a biangular one increases progeny;
a tri- (or three-) angular, a quadrangular, and a pentangular [stone] grant sons.
A hexangular [stone] is said to cause hatred; a heptangular one brings about [the destruction of] enemies; an octangular one grants food; and a decangular one is for the sake of prosperity.
The [mandala] with thirty-three sides is [auspicious].
The fifteen-sided one is fortunate, while the six-sided one bestows enjoyment.
The eight-sided is said to cause affliction, and the twelve-sided brings fear.
The sixteen-sided [liṅga] is for the sake of happiness, especially for practitioners;
it remains standing, seated, or reclining, and is endowed with the form of a liṅga.
The *liṅga* should be square and the *āsana* perfectly circular;
the *śayana*, however, is taught to have a root like that of *kuśa* grass and a thick tip.
The observer of the vow [attains] purity... a four-cornered [mandala];
the bed... of him... and in other [places], the moving and the unmoving.
For the sake of protecting all, especially in villages and other settlements,
a *liṅga* or an image embodying the Lord (*īśvara*) was established by the gods or sages according to the prescribed rite;
or it may be a self-manifested *liṅga* or an image of the nature of the Lord.
For that purpose, [at the time] equal to... || (F12a, 1st line) || the time for worship.
Vaiśyas and Śūdras who enter while initiated [should act thus]:
one may perform a sacrifice for one's own sake, but one must not perform it for the sake of another.
(Second line) That which is desired would be struck; its method is now being explained.

It has been taught by means of the triad, and then by means of the [remaining] triad; [these] are remembered as the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). Specifically, during each watch of the night, one should practice them individually.
And at night, during the dark fortnight, [he should perform] the supreme worship... for the sake of worship.
The worship performed according to the method described above shall be the most excellent of the excellent.
Then, [the worship] of the lamps at the four corners [is performed] by means of a hundred [offerings].
At night, however, one should perform the third [session]... and the middle and the highest.
In the four [periods] of transition, [there is] the second [session] at the transition of night...
(.... scattered throughout the six (.... especially;
(6th line) even in the agreement (.... all [the] streams (upa...).
The twilight [period] is always mixed; it is generally considered to belong to both [the pure and the impure].
[This concludes] the distinction regarding the worship of the pure and other [categories].
(... therein, O Janārdana, such is the certainty of the scripture concerning the two... of... ||

When the sun has risen... that is called the morning twilight (*pūrvasandhyā*), and it shall be the Great [Twilight] (*mahā-*) as well. Beyond that, during the half-watch (*ardhayāma*), worship is indeed offered by her.

It should be understood as "with the twilight" when performed at midday during the watch; that junction of midday is also known by the name "Great Twilight. Furthermore, the worship performed for half a watch thereafter is all-pervading.

That [Mahāsandhyā] also occurs at the two junctions of day and night (*upasandhyā*) within the four periods beginning with the afternoon (*ahiryāmya*). Thus, the two Mahāsandhyās have been described, followed by the two Upasandhyās.
These [Upasandhyās] begin at night and continue until the end of the day.
The worship [should be performed] at the junctions of the day (saṃdhyā) for half a watch (ardhayāma);
thereafter, one should likewise arrange the third [offering] for half a watch.
(... the channel (*nāḍī*) of the rising [sun] on the preceding day;

From that, O Prajāpati, a sprout emerged, and from it a stalk arose.

In the center of the head, the two ears, the base of the horns, the two eyes, the nose, the throat,
and the two lips; in the root of the palate,
the row of teeth, the heart, the navel, the testicles, and the penis.
And the bone-touching [wind] extends from the root of the tail to the middle of the chest.
One should place [the mantra] ending with the tip of the question; one should place it with the three atoms (*tryāṇu*).

"May we know him whose horns are sharp; may we meditate upon him whose feet are the Vedas; may that Bull impel us.
(3rd line) There, the wise one should perform the invocation according to the ritual procedure as before.

and at the conclusion of that, one should present an offering of food accompanied by side dishes.

likewise, one should offer well-cooked food in the ritual of the food offering (*naivedya*) and the rite of oblation (*balikarman*).
At the invocation and at the conclusion of the worship, having offered the great portion and the arghya,
one should perform the worship at the proper time with the supreme concealed cloth.
[The mind] of those afflicted by evil diseases, those fallen [from their path], and atheists... thus it is said.
(5th line) The day of the week of Durmukha and others is unfavorable for fools and is censured by the teachers.
(... Having sold the life-breaths of Brahmins, [and having performed] initiation and devotion as prescribed (... (6th line) ...
having performed fasting unto death, [the rite] is fruitless if devoid of worship.
Having consecrated the concealed cloth which cuts away all defects,
and having removed the curtain while reciting the heart-mantra.
One should insert the left hand into the right side of the door-panel;
thereafter, one should perform that [rite] for the mantras of the left [deities].
Having recited *sadyojātam*,
[one should worship] with the mantra "vāstoṣpate" in the southwest (*nairṛte*).
One should go to the inner sanctum (*garbhageha*) [of the deity]...
(2nd line) ...whether it be Svayambhū, Daivaka, Bāṇa, Gaṇa, or likewise Aṣaka.

The remaining [form] is known as the *liṅga*; there is no dismissal (*udvāsana*) for it during worship, especially in the case of the *śiṣṭaliṅga*. (3rd line) By the gods and the sages, [protection was granted] to beasts, birds, and deer; specifically, the *svāyambhuva* armor was provided. (4th line) Furthermore, whatever *liṅga* has been consecrated by the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and others— (5th line)
It is called the "remaining linga," which is the cause for the presence of Śiva.
For him, by the sequence of [the ritual] leading up to the marriage ceremony,
there shall be the blazing of the fire situated in the mandala through the wind.
And just as the Blessed Lord Śiva is generated by means of the mere *liṅga*,
having offered that [oblation], with palms joined and flowers cast, one should recite the *Prāsāda* mantra.
Through devotion, they have attained the state of being one with the Equal One (*samarasi*), whose sphere is the partless (*niṣkala*);
[they abide] in the abode of power (*śakti*) situated within the two steps, likewise in the resonance (*nāda*) and the point (*bindu*).
Having departed from the abode of Mātaspakti, he spoke thus:
"The nature of the mantras, the dwelling, the act of dwelling, and likewise the nature;
the dwelling of the nature of the phonemes, and the dwelling of the phonemes upon the tongue."

The tongue has its abode in the mouth, and the mouth has its abode in the intellect; the wise one [knows this]. The intellect has its abode in the heart, and the heart has its abode in the physical body (*piṇḍa*); the physical bodies have their abode in the channels (*nāḍī*), and the channels have their abode in the vital air (*vāyu*).
The dwelling of the powers through power, and the dwelling of Śiva... this is proclaimed as the dwelling of all mantras.
(This is declared to be the dwelling of mantras; it is called the vehicle of mantras.)
One should place that linga which is devoid of a sūtra upon the center of the head.
As many times as the linga has faces, so many shall be the mouths of the cave.
The self is the vehicle, and from that, the two vehicles of the sacrifice arise.
They remember the invocation, yet they forget the dismissal;
and even when the ritual is performed by those who know, it appears in various forms.
O Supreme Lord, having meditated upon the Teacher in one's mind according to one's desire—
In this way, milk of many colors becomes [of] one [taste];
likewise, a mantra born from a single source assumes many forms.
One should offer flowers worshipped during the morning twilight and dismiss them with the Īśāna-mantra.
The wise practitioner, taking a flower between the little finger,
the ring finger, and the middle finger, should discard the flower that has been sprinkled with water using the thumb and forefinger.
At the time of dismissal, however, one should cause that flower to be placed upon the heads [of the deities].
One should offer everything remaining from the worship to Caṇḍeśa.
One should indeed wash the liṅga with the Astra-mantra using the palm of the right hand; one should wash it all around in sequence with the Pīṭha-pāśupata-mantra.
Having sprinkled it with the water of the general arghya, one should perform the purification of the liṅga.

The fifth [requirement] is the purity of the mantra; the supreme instructor should cause this to be performed. Then, by moving a clod of earth [around the disciple], one effects the removal of the mantra’s impurity. Indeed, the mere utterance of the final *nāda* does not itself constitute the instigation of the mantra’s purification.

All mantras, especially those beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*, should be employed in the sacrifice; this is declared to be the purification of the mantra. Having understood the fivefold purification of the water, you are worthy to perform the worship.
In the movement of Indra during sacrifice, one would obtain that which is fruitless;
[but] when the moon and sun [are joined], it brings about all success and is auspicious.
The upward breath (*ūrdhvaprāṇa*) is likewise eternal, while the chariot-breath (*rathaprāṇa*) is the moon.
They go to hell for those two; for him, there is the destruction of the moon and the sun.
Having abandoned day and night, how can one who is unworthy be a teacher?
The eye consists of all beings; the moon and the sun abide within its function.
With a mind not distracted by anything else, the mind is purified by the two eyes.
O Prajāpati, the vision of the two eyes is focused right here;
as long as the worship is to be completed, one should remain there with the movement of the mind.

Since there is no other sight than this by which the supreme austerity of the Imperishable is attained, worship of the Lord of Gods is performed through that [sight] alone; the mind is not satisfied by any other form of worship. O best of the twice-born, that in which the functions of both the mind and the eyes reside—*
When the mind has thus become focused on that task, one should worship [it]...

it is said that the time for the sun and moon is the "time of the fire of time" (*kālorkakāla*). At the transition of the sun (*saṃkrānti*) or at the equinox (*viṣuva*), worship should never be performed.

The movement from one *puṭa* to another *puṭa* is called *saṃkrānti*. Likewise, the hollow space (*suṣira*) that has shifted between the two *puṭas* on both sides is proclaimed to be the dual downward breath (*apāna*) and indeed poison (*viṣa*).
One should not perform the emission of breath; one should maintain silence and worship [the deity] thoroughly.
Endowed with the conduct of the ancients, one should worship while remaining in the position of Agni.
One should worship [the deity] in the southwest, connected with the southern gate;
one should worship Adhisattva Nairṛta, connected with the western gate.
One should worship the northern gate in the direction of Vāyu;
and one should worship both the eastern and western [gates] facing north.
One should worship [the deity] facing east, whether in the north or in the south;
however, if one intends to invoke the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), one should worship the *liṅga* while seated.
Having thus performed the eightfold excellence and established the *liṅga*, one should worship the deity;
there, one should prepare a seat according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures.
The support is declared to be the seat (āsana), and that which is supported is the supreme Śiva.
Nāda is declared to be the liṅga, and bindu is remembered as the pedestal (pīṭha).
Śiva is never devoid of power; he is not without Śakti.
It should be understood that [power] is like fragrance in flowers, or like water in the ocean.
Therefore, one should worship the vital power (*prāṇa-śakti*) which resides within him.

Power alone is declared to be the seat (*āsana*), [consisting] of the five [elements] in sequence. The stalk is the mass of the earthly egg, and it is indeed the supreme vehicle. Having taken recourse to the foundational power (*ādhāra-śakti*), [one perceives] the emergence of the primary qualities, beginning with *dharma*.
Listen to the description of the form of the seat for the purpose of the visualization-offering (*dhyānapūjā*);
O Goddess, it is like the base of a string of pearls, consisting of both the letter *la* and the vowel *e*.
Having four faces and eight arms, resembling molten gold,
he [visualizes] the twelve-syllable [mantra] upon the lotus of his nose.
Seated upon his wife, he holds a spear, a noose, a goad, the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness,
a discus, a lotus, a javelin, and the gesture of supreme knowledge (*jñānamudrā*).
The wise Teacher should visualize her endowed with all ornaments, the singular excellence of the entire world;
he should visualize Śakti in the form of the support (*ādhāra*), within the interior of the seed-syllable of Śakti, as the stalk, the staff, and the source of the letters beginning with *ga*.
He should visualize Śakti as the syllables *ām* and *ām*, and the seed-syllable resembling the stride of Viṣṇu (*vikrama*).
Indeed, its stem has the luster of a polished gem, resembling lapis lazuli;
it is anointed with the practice of Dharma and established in the principles of Dharma and so forth.
Held in the hand by the foundational power (*ādhāra-śakti*), it is entirely free from all censure.
Then, first is the Anantāsana, the second is Siṃhāsana, the third is Yogāsana, and the fourth shall be Padmāsana. The fifth is named Vimala; these five consist of the nature of the five elements.
The seat is declared to be [the locus], and Paramaśiva is that which is to be placed upon it.
There, the seat is like the *bindu*, and Śiva is held to be like the *nāda*. Thus, when the two are joined, Śiva is revealed.
In the application of invocation and seating, there is the lion-throne;
in worship, the lotus called Vimala is for the meal.
Among those, the hymn (*stotra*) consisting of song and so forth is here called Anantāsana.
It is located in the east, or in the state [of the deity], or somewhat in the region of fire.
Takṣaka in the southern region, Kārkoṭaka in the southwest,
Śaṅkhapāla with the two arms, and Gulika in the domain of the wind.
The Padma [seat] is in the northern direction, and the Mahāpadma is in the northeast;
it should be circular, resting upon Ananta’s seat and supported by a tortoise.
Then one should encircle the central stalk and the fire of Śiva;
O Brahmin, listen now to the support and the deities of the sacrificial vessels.
From Ananteśa comes Sūkṣma; from Ekanetra comes Śivottama;
from Ekarudra comes Trimūrti; and from Śikhaṇḍin comes Śikhaṇḍa.
The preceptor, having sequentially deposited [the mantras] from the east to the northeast,
[should likewise place] the forms of the Vasus, the Nāgas, and the Indras— fourteen in total.
This has been declared as the Anantāsana; now hear the procedure for the Siṃhāsana.
Regarding the sequence of the Siṃhāsana: Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya constitute the fourfold [feet].
Dharma has the form of an elephant, and knowledge has the form of an elephant;
detachment shall have the form of a lion, and sovereignty the form of an elephant. He is protected individually by millions upon millions of lions.
A conch shell, yellow crystal, red, and the color of a lion— these four, namely the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), Necessity (*niyati*), Time (*kāla*), and [the fourth] Time (*kāla*),
should be arranged in sequence upon the four sides of the square board.
The auspicious lion-throne has Keśava as its middle foot, with the scales and the bull as its supports.
With three eyes and a terrifying appearance, it likewise possesses wide vision and valor.
Thus the lion-throne has been described; now hear about the yoga-throne.
In the four directions, however, there should be yoga; one should arrange the remainder as follows:
having established *prāṇa* in the east, one should place *apāna* in the domain of fire (*agni*).
One should place *vyāna* in the region of the wind (*vāyu*), and likewise *udāna* in the southwest (*nairṛta*).
The western [quarter] of this is the same, and likewise the Naga is in the northwest.
In the north, [the breath] is Kūrma; in the northeast, it is Kṛkara; in the southeast, it is Devadatta;
and in the south, it is Dhananjaya—thus it is scattered throughout the quarters.
I have now explained the support; listen now to the deity.
The Praṇava is in the middle region, while the letter *a* is in the eastern region.
The letter *i* is in the region of Agni, and likewise the letter *u* in the south;
the letter *o* is in the southwest, and the letter *ai* is in the west. The letter *ṛ* is in the region of Vāyu, while the letter *vi* is in the northern region.
The syllable *ne* is situated in the north-eastern direction, and the syllable *oṃ* is located in the eastern direction.
That which has no upper covering is known as the yogic seat (*yogāsana*). Thus, O Ām-Ū, the mouth of sacrifice has been declared to you; now hear the procedure for the lotus seat (*padmāsana*).
Earth is on the eastern petal, and water is in the direction of fire (the southeast).
The form of fire is in the south-east, while the form of wind is in the south-west.
O best of Brahmins, space (*ākāśa*) is said to be the petal in the western direction;
having placed *sattva* in the eastern direction and *tejas* in the northern direction,
O Brahmin, one should fashion that form upon the northeastern petal.
Endowed with the true colors, it is thus described by me.
One should fashion the root with the *sadyojāta* mantra and the stalk with the *vāmadeva* mantra.
[The *vāmadeva-brahma-mantra*:]
They say that the Aghora petal is indeed the Puruṣa, O secret ones.
The most excellent of teachers should perform [the rite] with the *saṣīramaka* mantra.
I shall now fully declare the deities; one should first place Kāla.
One should place Kalavikaraṇī in the southeast and Raudrī in the south;
Balavikaraṇī in the southwest and Vāmī in the west;
Amoghā in the northwest and Jyeṣṭhā and the others in the northern direction.
"O Sarvabhūta," [one should place] Manonmanī in the northeast, while [the central deity] is in the center.
Thus the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) has been explained; now hear the pure procedure.
One should perform the placement (*vinyāsa*) which has the nature of the four Vedas, and the meditation (*dhyāna*) like a skin.
Having placed [the syllables] upon the Amalīka stone, listen now to [the arrangement] of the deities:
Ambī should be established in the east, and Gaṇāmbī in the south.
Having placed Gaurī in the west and [the other goddesses] in the northern direction, this is declared to be the Vimalāsana; now listen to another.
The preceptor should worship well with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps,
using the first syllable of each person's own name and the heart-mantra.
One should arrange the qualities of rajas and tamas one above the other;
and within the circle of fire, at its conclusion, is the circle of the sun.
Thereafter, one should place the lunar disc, and within it, the Self and the Inner Self;
likewise, one should perform the placement of the Supreme Self by means of the [respective] locations.
On the right is the principle of the Self (*ātmatattva*), and on the left is the principle of Knowledge (*vidyātattva*).
One should then place the Śiva-tattva in the center according to the proper sequence.
Having thus performed the ritual placement according to rule, one should then worship Śiva,
as well as the self-existent [deity], the preceptor, and the divine, the measure, and the human.
The Rākṣasa and the Bāṇa-liṅga are said to be the sevenfold liṅgas;
one should arrange a single seat for the Svayambhū, Devika, and Bāṇa liṅgas.
In the *ārṣa* [tradition] one should arrange three seats, and in the *gāṇapa* [tradition] likewise; it is recorded in tradition that in the *mānuṣa* [tradition] five seats should be prepared.
If the worship consists of a single enclosure (*ekāvaraṇa*), one should arrange five seats. That secret, single-syllable [mantra] is indeed proclaimed to be the *praṇava*.
Know him, O Janārdana, to be the three qualities, the three worlds,
the three gods, the three times, and the three principles.

Two types of Brahman have been taught: the Brahman of Sound (śabdabrahman) and the Supreme Brahman. That Supreme Brahman is designated as Śiva, who exists as the essence of the word "Brahman" (Sadāśiva).
That which consists of the Śabdabrahman is remembered as Sadāśiva;
O Janārdana, Sadāśiva is the manifest body of the Praṇava. Filling his joined palms with flowers, Sthirayus, with senses restrained, [worshipped].
One should assign Sadāśiva to the liṅga and worship Maheśa in the image.
The invisible one is called "the visible" within the orbs of Rāhu, the Moon, and the Sun;
it is seen as if engaged in combat with the Self, or even as standing still.
O Six-faced One, when the stainless iron is invisible and devoid of consciousness,
both you and I perceive that the Supreme Self and the self are indeed stainless.
In the same way, having understood the nature of form within the center of the body—
just as fire exists in the middle of wood, or as water exists at the edge of a body of water— so it is there.
As long as the sun-gem remains intact, it is blue; when it is broken, it is smeared [with colors]. As long as there is luster within the gem, so too is there light within the density, like a flame.
Just as iron is known to exist within stone, and ghee within milk,
so too, O Guha, from the end of the night until sunrise, there is indeed that very rising [of the sun].
Following the path of the guru’s instruction, the invocation occurs through recollection;
it is endowed with fifteen eyes and joined with five heads.
Having two feet and ten arms, endowed with excellent sacrificial threads,
wearing an upper garment of tiger skin, and adorned with armlets and bracelets.
Adorned with a necklace of seed-pods (*karṇikā*), bracelets, a waist-belt, and a girdle;
endowed with five faces and possessed of five tongues.
Each face has three eyes, and [the hands] are adorned with all kinds of jewel rings;
in the right [hands], there is the gesture of fearlessness, a vajra, a sword, a trident, and an axe.
Having meditated upon the form— with the serpent, the spittle, the letter, and fire on the left side of the boon-granter—
shining like a jasmine flower, the moon, or crystal, and adorned with a crown of matted locks,
one should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) therein according to what was previously stated.

Through meditation, all persons attain liberation, supreme bliss, and that which is beyond sorrow. Some obtain perfection (*siddhi*) with this very body, as well as enjoyments and a form at the time of dissolution.
With that same handful of flowers and with this mantra, the teacher—
O Maheśvara, I shall now explain the sequence of the paths and their specific distinctions:
the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan), the path of words (padādhvan), the path of principles (tattvādhvan), and the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan).
The path of mantra and the path of kalā are its essential nature;
the path of phonemes, as previously described, is its skin, and the path of words is likewise its head.
The path of principles is its heart, while the path of worlds is its body hair.
The path of mantra, the path of blood, and that which consists of semen, marrow, and bone;
likewise, the path of *kalā* with all its limbs—thus is the form of the Ineffable (*sādākhya*).
Having invoked Śakti into the sacred seat (*pīṭha*), it is described as being of that very form.
The sandal and the shoe, as well as that which moves upon the earth;
the earth is to be known as the *kumuda*, while the neck is said to be formed by the two arms.
The throat is declared to be "kaṇṭha," and then the lower lip would be "re... (5th line);
likewise, the great cloth-head and the head of the enemy.
The mantra-practitioner should recite the tantra-mantra; she has two eyes and is endowed with two arms.
She is red in color, possesses the triple-bend posture (*tribhaṅga*), and is draped in variegated garments.
Adorned with all ornaments, she has full thighs, hips, and breasts.
Adorned with anklets, joined by a girdle upon her hips, fair-faced, enriched with perfumes and flowers, and decorated with hair-ornaments;
the goddess, wearing lotus petals, holds in her hands the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
[The mantra for invocation] || Likewise, the worship with mantras.
Having meditated thus, she, being afflicted, should contemplate Gaurī;
she should then perform the placement of the twenty-five kalās upon the body of Gaurī.
One should arrange the letters from *a* to *kṣa* as before;
then, in due order, [one should visualize the deity] seated, or well-rounded, or standing, or lying down.
At the time of worship, [the deity] is seated comfortably; at other times, as before.
Having invoked [the deity], one should then perform the rites of installation and so forth.
Then one should invoke the deity with the Sadyojāta mantra;
one should establish him with the Aghora mantra, and effect his presence [with the Vāmadeva mantra].
With the Īśāna mantra, the ancillary limbs (aṅga) should be assigned.

When Śiva has arrived, one should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) with the *hṛdaya* mantra, saying, "This is the foot-water for [the Lord] here. One should offer water for sipping (*ācamana*) into the [mouth-]cavities and place the respectful offering (*arghya*) upon the head.
Furthermore, one should first perform the ritual placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*) consisting of thirty-eight [syllables].
Having fumigated with guggulu resin and clarified butter while reciting the *Hṛdaya* mantra and the sound of the bell,
they should each separately recite the *Śrīsūkta*, the *Rudrasaṃkhyā*, and the *Camaka* hymn.
All the Brahmins, with their minds solely intent on recitation and meditation, performed the Narasūkta and other hymns in due order, while adorned with sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads.
May she who is Vaidikī, known as Śāntā and Śuddhā, [be present] through her compassion for all living beings.
[The food offering.]
He is skilled in training horses, dexterous, of noble lineage, endowed with excellent qualities, and a generous giver.
One who knows the Dharma, is possessed of statesmanship, is learned in the scriptures, has sons, and is free from anger;
one who is devoted to the Tantric treatises, has reached the further shore of the sciences of knowledge,
recognizes the authority of the Guru’s words, and has mastered the science of architecture.
Having observed the barley and other materials, one should perform the recitation according to the prescribed rule.
The preceptor, having uttered the mantra "Vyomavyāpin" with its ten syllables,
as well as the five Brahmans, the six limbs, and the letters beginning with the Mātṛkās;
The consecration should be performed separately for each using the Śiva-mantra;
likewise for the Śivāstra, the Kṣurikā, and the Śakti-weapon.
The Pāśupata weapon, and likewise the Aghora weapon—these five;
thus one should write and install the mantra of the five weapons in their proper sequence.
One should install the temple, the Praṇava, and the Sūtra-mantra;
likewise, one should install the Pāṇi-mantra, the Mūla-mantra, and the Jvālā-mantras.
The eighty-one great mantras, as well as those with joined syllables,
and the thousand-syllable *Vaivatsa* mantra, the *Mahāsoma*,
the *Aporāja* mantra, and likewise the *Tryambaka* mantra.
One should perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) with a measure equal to the tip of a cow’s horn.

In the performance of daily and occasional rites, in the accomplishment of mantras,
when there is an inauspicious birth-star for a king or others, or when one is afflicted by mental distress and the like;
The *rāvarti* [constellation] is auspicious for a king at the time of death when it coincides with his birth asterism;
it is also suitable for the commencement of battle on a constellation that brings victory to kings.
On the eighth lunar day of the moon, under the constellation Aṣṭatā, and likewise on the Vaiṇāśika [day],
at the conclusion of the initiation, at the conclusion of the installation, during the sprinkling, and during the burning of the city.
In the event of excessive rain, drought, [famine], or a field being submerged;
during an earthquake, the burning of the quarters, or even when oppressed by enemies;
at the conclusion of a sacrifice, on a Sunday, or on days with an unfavorable son [in the horoscope]; (4th line) [one should perform the rite].
(... during eclipses, at great portents, and during great festivals in one's own fields;
at the solstices, at the equinoxes, during lunar and solar eclipses, when the *liṅga* is newly installed, and also at the rite of offering the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*).
At the time of the lighting of the Kṛttikās, or during another lunar mansion,
on the eighth, the fourteenth, and the fifteenth— the holy festival days—
as well as at the transit of the sun and during the Ṣaḍaśītimukha.

At the commencement of the [planetary] retrogression, during an auspicious conjunction, at the conclusion of the chariot festival, at the end of the arrival of new waters, and at the conclusion of the river [festival]... || 3 ||
Especially on the full moon day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa under the asterism Ārdrā, during all rites of expiation, in the offering of fresh food,
at times of human auspiciousness, and at the moment of death;
Especially at the time of worship, during the festivals of the [Buddhas] who have attained parinirvāṇa,
at the conclusion of the circumambulation of the deity, and at the end of a hunting expedition—
at such times as these, one should perform the ritual bathing as prescribed for the ablution.
One should perform this daily, or else at the three junctions of the day for the supreme guru;
thereafter, one should cause the ritual bathing to be performed twice or even once.
That [method] is now described as being performed by reducing the number two-by-two according to the previously mentioned path;
or else, one should bathe [the deity] with one hundred and eight, or eighty-one, or twenty-eight, sixteen, or nine [units], starting from nine and increasing up to one hundred and eight.
At the moments of rebirth, by means of a single jar, [or] by means of space, [or] by means of number...

One should carefully avoid [the following types of vessels]: those containing the substances previously mentioned along with the *vardhanī* vessel; those that have been cracked, porous, chipped, or broken; those that are sunken; those that are scorched; and those that are old.
All of them resemble ripe bimba fruits; one should wash them with particular care.
One should encircle [the site] with three layers of dark-colored jars in sequence;
or else, one should encircle it for the third time with a thread of the sky.
One, two, or three *yava*s [in height], the *kumbha* and the *vardhanī*;
and other jars (*kalaśa*) with openings resembling lattice windows (*gavākṣa*).
Then, having wrapped it all over with thread, and also upon a svastika, one should place the jars encircled by threads; if it is for the increase of enemies, it should be done in that same manner.
Likewise, [the jar] thus encircled is considered to be the expiation.
To the north of the pavilion, the wise man should spread darbha grass and flowers;
having encircled it with a thread, he should then wash [it].
One should place the water-pots (kalaśas) there with their openings facing downward upon *kuśa* grass.
One should sprinkle [them] with the Heart-mantra and perform the sprinkling (*abhiṣecana*) upon the pot.
Adorned with all ornaments, one should then install that [deity]... [there].
One should purify the ground two or three times with [water] mixed with *pañcagavya*.
The third [step] is the laying out of the threads; the fourth shall be the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
The fifth is the ritual placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*); by means of the recitation of the hymn (*ṛc*), the sixth [is performed].
The seventh is the arrangement of substances, the eighth is the placement of deities;
the ninth is declared to be the ritual procedure, and the tenth is the wrapping with cloth.
The eleventh is the offering of fragrant flowers, and the twelfth is incense and lamps.
The thirteenth is said to be the mudrā, while the fourteenth is the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*).
The fifteenth is the raising of the water-pot, and at the sixteenth, one should bathe Śiva.
One should purify the ground with the Astra mantra and smear it with the Vāmadeva mantra.
One should perform the laying of the lines with the Aghora mantra and the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with the Puruṣa mantra.
One should place the water-pot (*kumbha*) with the Hṛdaya mantra and the seat (*sāna*) with the Īśāna mantra.
One should arrange the ritual substances with the *mūla-mantra*, invoke the deities with the left [hand],
place the bowls with the principal seed-syllable (*bīja*), and the garments with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
[One should offer] the nine perfumes, incense, and so forth with the *kavaca-mantra*.
One should offer the mudrā with the *aghora* mantra and cause [the officiant] to recite the *pavamāna* hymn.
With the remainder of the [offering], one should [recite] the *puṇyāha* for the Arhats.
One should perform the lifting of the jar (*ghaṭoddhāra*) with the *praṇava* and with the mantra "Mahāvyoma."
[The Sequence of Empowerment]
One should bathe the Supreme Lord with [the substances] beginning with *gandha*—
three, five, seven, eight, nine, eleven, twelve, ten,
or nine times; thus the form [of the ritual] becomes manifold.
That which is joined with Agasti is called the Jagaticchanda.
(3rd line) [That which is] joined with [the other] is called the supreme triad.
With the feet situated on the threads and the knees situated in the corners, the hands are placed in the middle. (4th line)
They have [u]... hands, and they hold water-jars in their hands;
all are three-eyed and four-armed, two-legged, and adorned with [ornaments] beginning with [the elephant-girdle]. Holding a water-jar in the left hand, they cover it with [their right hand].
And having held the *ṭaṅka* [instrument] in the other [hand], [he performs] the sprinkling of the disciple (*ṣiṣya*).
Having thus meditated upon Rudra’s portion, the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśas*), and Īśvara with Ambikā,
the Preceptor (*deśika*) establishes [the disciple] facing east and ties his topknot (*śikhā*).

But for the other gods, [the ritual] should likewise face toward Śiva. Having placed the mantras... [and] having addressed the Rudras, one should again perform the consecration with those very [mantras] in due order.
[The Ritual for Fruit and Water]
Oil produced by a hand-press, combined with fragrant flowers.

One should rub the Śiva-mantra upon the pedestal of the *liṅga*. Having repeatedly smeared the *liṅga* together with its altar (*vedikā*) in due order, using flour made from rice, millet, wild rice, barley, beans, and so forth... (2nd line) ... [one should proceed].
By following the king’s command, with fragrant *āmalaka* and other such substances—(3rd line)—namely, fragrant *āmalaka*, *lakṣmī*, and likewise *haridrā*:
by means of these three, the supreme bath [is performed]... and the *āmalaka* [attains its purpose]. (4th line)

The medium bath is intended for one who is not afflicted by illness; with half a *rudrākṣa* [bead], he should bathe [the deity] with pleasantly warm water, or even with milk, and then [one] should perform the [subsequent rite].
With *bilva* leaves and a bath of clarified butter, the preceptor [obtains the merit of] ten cows.
Having given thousands [of gifts], he attained that state which is difficult to reach.
One obtains all that fruit when the anointing of the *liṅga* has been performed;
[this applies] when the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) have been used at the conclusion of the ritual.
At the end of the coconut [vessel], there is the essence of the fruit;
at the end of that, flower-water; and at the end of that, [the water] of the *ma...*.
At the end of that, water with *kuśa* grass; at the end of that, scented water.
According to one's means, [offer these] to Hari.
But at the conclusion of each substance, one should perform a bath with incense;
he who, having thus consecrated the Liṅga, then performs [the rite]...
He who, having bathed [the image] with curds, worships it with devotion, is honored in the world of Rudra for ten million times ten million aeons.
...for twenty aeons he is glorified in the world of Śiva;
that man who bathes the *liṅga* with water [mixed] with milk...
By means of the royal celestial chariot (*vimāna*), he is glorified in the world of Soma. One should perform the consecration with the waters of cows and worship with devotion. (End of ṚE32608.
